title: A Parish for the Ledger
premise: Silas Winterbourne, a retired detective hiding behind the counter of a failing seaside bookshop, has quietly solved three deaths the police ruled accidents, keeping her gift invisible to protect her found family of misfit regulars. When a nervous stranger pays a year's rent in advance to prove that a murder has not yet happened, Silas discovers the man is already dead and his death is pre-written in an antique parish ledger sold through her own shop. Following the ledger's coded entries toward the drowned church at Graywater Point, she uncovers a conspiracy among the town's founding families who have been 'predicting' deaths to seize land for generations. In the end Silas must choose between exposing the truth and losing the only home she has left, and she does both: she burns the ledger's power by publishing it, adopts the client's orphaned daughter into her ragtag household, and lets the tide take the last page.
about_author: Jude Dunmore is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing coastal burial records before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about quiet towns where the paperwork remembers more than the people do.

chapters.title: The Rent Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Silas Winterbourne, POV. A gaunt stranger named Edmund Vail pays a year's rent on her failing bookshop to hire her for an impossible job: prove that no murder has happened yet. Silas, wary but broke, accepts. The emotional beat is uneasy curiosity — the first crack in her carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Hand
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Flashback chapter establishing how she quietly solved three deaths the police called accidents, aided by her irregular family: ferryman Tomás, teenage runaway Wren, and insomniac vicar Mrs. Okonkwo. The beat is warmth shadowed by fear that being seen again will cost her everything.

chapters.title: A Ledger Sold Twice
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Sorting stock, Wren realizes the antique parish ledger Silas sold last month was bought back days later by a stranger — and that pages have been replaced with facsimiles. The beat is dawning dread as the shop itself becomes evidence.

chapters.title: The Man Who Was Already Dead
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas visits Vail's address to report progress and finds him dead, staged as a heart attack, with a fresh ledger entry predicting his death dated three weeks prior. The beat is cold fury: someone used her shop as cover and expects her to stay silent.

chapters.title: Graywater Point
chapters.summary: Tomás, POV. Ferrying Silas to the drowned church ruins, Tomás reveals locals avoid the point since the Harrow family bought the shoreline. He confesses he's been paid to stop asking questions. The beat is loyalty tested against terror.

chapters.title: Entries in a Dead Hand
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Comparing the ledger's predictions with parish death records, Silas finds nine 'foretold' deaths across sixty years — all accurate, all profitable to landholders. The beat is intellectual exhilaration curdling into horror at the pattern's patience.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okonkwo, POV. The old vicar admits she recognized the ledger years ago and stayed silent because her predecessor was its keeper — and died for it. She gives Silas the cipher key hidden in a hymnal. The beat is guilt finally set down like a heavy bag.

chapters.title: Wren Follows Someone
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Ignoring orders, Wren tails a well-dressed man photographing the shop and loses him near the Harrow estate, but photographs his car. The beat is reckless bravery and the first hint the family knows Silas is looking.

chapters.title: An Offer of Silence
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Cordelia Harrow visits the bookshop, charming and venomous, offering to buy the building outright if Silas returns the ledger and forgets Vail. The beat is temptation sharpened into threat; Silas realizes the rent money was bait from the start.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gave Back
chapters.summary: Tomás, POV. After a storm, the sea exposes a coffin from the drowned churchyard containing not bones but ledgers — decades of them, the family's true archive. The beat is awe and dread: the conspiracy's memory is physical, and now it's loose.

chapters.title: The Cipher Breaks
chapters.summary: Silas and Wren, alternating POV. Working through the night, they decode the entries: each 'prediction' was a schedule, and the next name written is Wren's. The beat is protective panic — Silas's found family has become the target.

chapters.title: Police, Politely
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Silas takes her evidence to Inspector Dane, who once dismissed her 'accidents,' and finds him compromised — Harrow money built his career. He warns her off while slipping her one useful file. The beat is disillusionment confirming the theme: justice won't come from the law.

chapters.title: The Empty Shop
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Returning to find the bookshop ransacked and Mrs. Okonkwo missing, Wren must decide whether to run or fight. The beat is fear transmuted into resolve; Wren hides the hymnal cipher where only family would look.

chapters.title: Hymns and Hostages
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. A ransom note trades Mrs. Okonkwo for the recovered ledgers. Silas negotiates by phone, buying time while Tomás scouts the exchange site at the ruined church. The beat is controlled rage beneath a negotiator's calm.

chapters.title: The Exchange at the Drowned Church
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. At Graywater Point, Silas hands over decoy books; the handoff collapses when Cordelia's enforcer recognizes the forgery. Mrs. Okonkwo is freed in the chaos but Silas is captured. The beat is sacrifice — invisibility abandoned completely.

chapters.title: The Family Business
chapters.summary: Cordelia, POV. Held in the Harrow house, Silas hears Cordelia explain the creed: the ledger doesn't predict deaths, it schedules them, and the family are merely stewards of an older covenant. The beat is chilling conviction — the villain believes she is the law.

chapters.title: Wren's Long Night
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Refusing to wait, Wren uses the cipher's final key — the original ledger page Silas kept hidden in the shop's false shelf — to decode the location of the covenant's proof-of-deeds archive, then calls Tomás. The beat is the student becoming the rescuer.

chapters.title: Rising Tide
chapters.summary: Tomás and Wren, alternating POV. Racing the incoming tide through the flooded crypt beneath the church, they reach Silas as her captors move her to be 'an entry.' The beat is desperate momentum, water rising, lanterns failing.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Confronting Cordelia in the crypt, Silas turns the ledger's logic against her: the final entry names Cordelia herself, written by her own paranoid father. The enforcers waver; the tide breaches. The beat is the trap closing on its author.

chapters.title: What the Water Takes
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. As the crypt floods, Cordelia drowns clutching the ledger rather than let go of it; Silas saves the enforcer who hesitated, choosing mercy over symmetry. The beat is grief without triumph — justice done, but nothing clean about it.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. With Dane disgraced, a new inspector takes Silas's full testimony; the surviving Harrow holdings are seized, and the ledgers enter evidence. Silas declines credit, letting the record speak. The beat is quiet vindication — justice outside the law, then handed back to it.

chapters.title: Open for Business
chapters.summary: Silas, POV. Spring: the bookshop reopens with Wren behind the counter, Mrs. Okonkwo leading story hour, and Vail's orphaned daughter asleep in the reading chair — the newest member of the family. A stranger enters with a strange request. Silas smiles. The beat is belonging earned, and the door left open.
